topic: How train wheels stay on the track

concept.title: Coned wheels steer through curves
concept.description: Train wheels are slightly conical and fixed to a solid axle; sideways shift changes each wheel's rolling radius.
assessmentCriteria: Explains how the cone shape lets the outer wheel travel farther in a curve

promptMarkdown: A train's two wheels are fixed to one solid axle, so they must turn at the same rate. Yet in a curve the outer rail is longer than the inner one. Explain how the wheels cope without slipping.

rubric.criterion: States that the wheels are conical (tapered)
Explains that the wheelset shifts sideways so the outer wheel rolls on a larger radius and the inner on a smaller one
Connects larger rolling radius to more distance per rotation

idealAnswer: The wheel treads are slightly conical. In a curve the wheelset shifts toward the outside, so the outer wheel rides on a wider part of its cone and the inner wheel on a narrower part. Both turn at the same rate, but the outer wheel's larger rolling radius covers more distance per turn, matching the longer outer rail. Flanges are only a backup.

answers.text: The wheels aren't cylinders, they're slightly cone shaped. Going round a bend the whole axle slides a little toward the outside, which puts the outer wheel on the fat part of its cone and the inner wheel on the thin part. Same number of turns, but the outer wheel has a bigger circumference where it touches the rail so it travels farther, which is exactly what the longer outer rail needs.

wheels r cone shape. in curve axel move to outside so outside wheel run on its biger part, inside wheel on smaler part. biger circle = more distanse each turn so outside one go further with same spining
The wheels are tapered, which keeps the train centered on the track and helps it go around curves.
The flanges on the inside edges of the wheels press against the rail and guide the train around the curve, and the wheels slip a tiny bit to make up the difference.
The outer wheel spins faster than the inner wheel in the curve, the same way a car's differential lets the outside wheel turn faster.

concept.title: Mutable default arguments
concept.description: Default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so a mutable default is shared across calls.
assessmentCriteria: Predicts the shared-list behaviour and explains when defaults are evaluated

promptMarkdown:
```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)
print(add(2))
```
What does this print, and why?

rubric.criterion: States the output is [1, 2]
Explains the default list is created once at definition time and shared between calls

idealAnswer: It prints [1, 2]. The default value [] is evaluated once, when the def statement runs, so every call that omits bucket appends to the same list object. The usual fix is bucket=None and creating a new list inside the function.

answers.text: [1, 2]. The empty list default is built a single time when Python defines the function, not on each call, so the first call's 1 is still in it when the second call appends 2.
It prints [1, 2] because the function remembers the list.
It prints [2]. Each call that doesn't pass bucket gets a brand new empty list, so only the 2 is in it.

concept.title: What a p-value means
concept.description: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
assessmentCriteria: States the conditional meaning and avoids the 'probability the null is true' reading

promptMarkdown: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for the difference in conversion rate. In one or two sentences, what does that number mean?

rubric.criterion: Says it is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were really no difference (null true)
Does not claim it is the probability that the null hypothesis is true or that the result is due to chance

idealAnswer: If there were truly no difference between A and B, we would see a difference at least this large about 3% of the time. It is not the probability that there is no real difference.

answers.text: Assuming the two versions actually convert the same, you'd get a gap this big or bigger only about 3 times in 100 experiments just from random variation.
It means there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true, so we can be 97% sure version B is really better.

answers.kind: true but doesn't say what it means
answers.text: It's below 0.05, so the result is statistically significant.

The p-value is a rigorous, well-established measure of practical importance. A value of 0.03 tells us that the treatment improved conversion by roughly three percent relative to control, and because this figure is derived from the full sample it reflects the magnitude of the underlying effect rather than sampling noise, which is why practitioners rely on it to size the business impact of a change.

concept.title: Why antibiotics don't work on viruses
concept.description: Antibiotics target structures and processes specific to bacteria; viruses lack them and replicate inside host cells.
assessmentCriteria: Explains the mechanism: antibiotics hit bacterial targets viruses don't have

promptMarkdown: Why doesn't an antibiotic help with a cold or the flu?

rubric.criterion: Says colds and flu are caused by viruses, not bacteria
Explains that antibiotics act on bacterial structures or machinery (cell wall, ribosomes, enzymes) that viruses do not have
Notes viruses replicate using the host cell's machinery

idealAnswer: Colds and flu are viral. Antibiotics work by attacking things bacteria have, such as their cell walls or their own ribosomes. Viruses have none of these; they copy themselves using our own cells' machinery, so there is nothing for the antibiotic to hit.

answers.text: Those are viruses. Antibiotics kill bacteria by breaking things like the bacterial cell wall or jamming bacterial ribosomes. A virus has no cell wall or ribosomes of its own, it hijacks your cells to copy itself, so the drug has no target.
Because colds and flu are viruses, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.
Cold and flu viruses have become resistant to antibiotics because people overused them for years.
Viruses are too small for the antibiotic molecules to find and attach to.

concept.title: Compound interest
concept.description: With compounding, each period's interest is added to the balance and itself earns interest.
assessmentCriteria: Computes a two-period compound balance and explains interest on interest

promptMarkdown: You put $1,000 in an account paying 10% a year, compounded annually. How much is there after 2 years, and why is it more than $1,200?

rubric.criterion: Gives $1,210
Explains that second-year interest is earned on $1,100, i.e. on the first year's interest too

idealAnswer: $1,210. After year one the balance is $1,100; year two's 10% is charged on $1,100, giving $110 rather than $100. The extra $10 is interest earned on the first year's interest.

answers.text: $1,210. Year 1 gives 100, so you have 1,100. Year 2 is 10% of 1,100 = 110. The extra 10 is interest on last year's interest.
$1,200, because 10% of 1,000 is 100 and you get that twice.
1000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 1210. It beats 1200 because the second 10% applies to 1100, not the original 1000.

concept.title: Why ice floats
concept.description: Hydrogen bonding holds water molecules in an open lattice in ice, making it less dense than liquid water.
assessmentCriteria: Links the open hydrogen-bonded structure of ice to its lower density

promptMarkdown: Most solids sink in their own liquid, but ice floats on water. Explain why, in terms of what the molecules are doing.

rubric.criterion: States ice is less dense than liquid water
Explains that in ice hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open, spaced-out lattice
Contrasts with liquid water, where molecules pack closer together

idealAnswer: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock each molecule into a rigid, open hexagonal lattice that holds the molecules farther apart than they are in the liquid, where bonds keep breaking and molecules can crowd closer. The same mass takes up more volume, so ice is less dense and floats.

answers.text: In liquid water the molecules tumble around and can squeeze close together. When it freezes the hydrogen bonds fix every molecule in a hexagonal framework with a lot of empty space in it, so the same water takes up about 9% more room. Less dense, so it floats.
Ice is less dense than water because the molecules spread out when it freezes.
Ice has tiny air bubbles trapped inside it when it freezes, and the air makes it lighter than the water.
When molecules get cold they slow down and weigh less, so the ice is lighter than the warmer water under it.

concept.title: What HTTPS protects
concept.description: HTTPS (TLS) provides encryption, integrity and server authentication; it does not provide anonymity or vouch for the site's honesty.
assessmentCriteria: Names what HTTPS protects and one thing it does not

promptMarkdown: You connect to a site over HTTPS on public Wi-Fi. What does HTTPS protect you from, and what is one thing it does NOT protect you from?

rubric.criterion: Says others on the network cannot read the traffic (encryption)
Mentions tampering protection or that the certificate verifies you are talking to the real site
Gives a valid limitation: e.g. the site itself may be malicious, the domain you visit is still visible, or it does not make you anonymous

idealAnswer: HTTPS encrypts the connection so people on the Wi-Fi cannot read or alter what you send and receive, and the certificate confirms you reached the real domain. It does not hide which site you are visiting, and it says nothing about whether the site itself is honest or safe.

answers.text: Other people on the Wi-Fi can't read my passwords or change the page on its way to me, and the certificate proves it's really that domain. But they can still see which site I'm connecting to, and a scam site can have HTTPS too.
It encrypts the data.
It hides your IP address and makes you anonymous so nobody can tell what sites you visit. It doesn't protect you from slow Wi-Fi.
HTTPS means the site has been checked and is safe, so it protects you from viruses and scams. It doesn't protect you if your battery dies.

concept.title: Axial tilt causes seasons
concept.description: Seasons come from Earth's axial tilt changing the angle and duration of sunlight, not from distance to the Sun.
assessmentCriteria: Attributes seasons to tilt via sunlight angle/day length, and rejects distance

promptMarkdown: Why is it summer in the Northern Hemisphere in June?

rubric.criterion: Attributes it to Earth's axial tilt, with the north tilted toward the Sun in June
Explains the effect: more direct sunlight and/or longer days
Does not attribute it to Earth being closer to the Sun

idealAnswer: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees. In June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer, which heats it more. Distance is not the cause: Earth is actually farthest from the Sun in early July.

answers.text: The Earth's axis is tilted. In June the top half leans toward the Sun, so the Sun is higher in the sky, the light hits more directly and the days are longer. It's not about distance, we're actually farthest from the Sun around then.
Because in June the Earth's orbit brings it closer to the Sun, so it gets hotter.
Because of the tilt of the Earth.
The Earth is tilted, so in June the Northern Hemisphere is closer to the Sun than the Southern Hemisphere and gets more heat.

concept.title: WHERE vs HAVING
concept.description: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
assessmentCriteria: Distinguishes row filtering before aggregation from group filtering after

promptMarkdown: In a query with GROUP BY, what is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

rubric.criterion: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping/aggregation
HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can use aggregate functions

idealAnswer: WHERE removes rows before they are grouped, so it cannot use aggregates like COUNT(*). HAVING is applied after GROUP BY, to whole groups, and can filter on aggregate results, e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.

answers.text: WHERE throws out rows before the grouping happens. HAVING runs after the groups are built, so it's where you put conditions on things like SUM or COUNT, e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.
HAVING is the one you use with GROUP BY.
WHERE filters the groups after they're aggregated, and HAVING filters the raw rows before grouping.
They do the same thing. HAVING is just older syntax that some databases still support.

concept.title: Ser vs estar
concept.description: Ser expresses identity and inherent characteristics; estar expresses states, conditions and location.
assessmentCriteria: States the distinction and gives a correct example of each

promptMarkdown: Spanish has two verbs for "to be". Explain when to use *ser* and when to use *estar*, with one example sentence for each.

rubric.criterion: Ser: identity, inherent characteristics, origin, profession or time
Estar: temporary states, conditions, feelings or location
Gives a correct example of each

idealAnswer: Ser is for what something is: identity, profession, origin, inherent traits, time (Soy profesora. Es de México.). Estar is for how or where something is: states, feelings, location (Estoy cansada. Madrid está en España.).

answers.text: Ser is for what something is, like identity, job, where you're from: "Ella es médica." Estar is for how it is right now or where it is: "Estoy cansado", "El libro está en la mesa."
Ser se usa para la identidad, la profesión, el origen y las características propias: "Mi hermano es alto." Estar se usa para estados, emociones y ubicación: "Hoy estoy enfermo" y "Estamos en casa."
Ser is for permanent things and estar is for temporary things.
Estar is for identity and permanent facts, like "Estoy profesor." Ser is for feelings and location, like "Soy cansado" and "Soy en casa."

concept.title: Vaccines train immune memory
concept.description: A vaccine presents a harmless antigen so the immune system builds antibodies and memory cells for a faster response later.
assessmentCriteria: Explains antigen exposure leading to immune memory

promptMarkdown: In a few sentences, how does a vaccine protect you from a disease you have not had yet?

rubric.criterion: Says the vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form or piece of the pathogen (an antigen)
Says the body responds by making antibodies and memory cells
Says this makes the response to the real pathogen faster or stronger

idealAnswer: A vaccine presents the immune system with a harmless version or piece of the pathogen. The body responds as if infected, producing antibodies and long-lived memory cells. If the real pathogen arrives later, those memory cells recognise it and respond quickly, often before you get ill.

answers.text: It gives your immune system a safe preview, a weakened germ or just a piece of it. Your body makes antibodies against it and keeps memory cells around, so when the real thing shows up it's recognised straight away and dealt with much faster.
It helps your body learn to fight the disease so you don't get as sick.
The vaccine contains antibodies that stay in your blood and kill the virus as soon as it gets in.

topic: History of ball bearings in bicycles

concept.title: Rolling instead of sliding
concept.description: Ball bearings replace sliding friction between axle and hub with much lower rolling friction.
assessmentCriteria: Explains the sliding-to-rolling change as the reason for lower friction

promptMarkdown: Why does putting ball bearings between a bicycle's axle and hub make the wheel spin so much more freely than a plain axle in a sleeve?

rubric.criterion: Says a plain sleeve means surfaces slide against each other
Says the balls roll between the two surfaces, replacing sliding with rolling
Notes rolling resistance is far lower than sliding friction, or that contact areas are tiny

idealAnswer: In a plain sleeve the axle surface slides against the hub, and sliding friction is high. With ball bearings the balls roll between the inner and outer races, so the surfaces no longer rub; rolling resistance is far lower than sliding friction, and each ball touches at only a tiny point.

answers.text: Without bearings the axle rubs against the inside of the hub the whole time, that's sliding friction. With balls in between nothing slides, the balls just roll between the two rings, and rolling takes far less force than dragging surfaces across each other.
The balls make it turn smoother so there's less friction.
The balls are made of a smoother, more slippery steel than the axle, so they slide past each other more easily.
